doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Meeting Django Reinhardt in Paris
summary: Carter found Django quiet and shy and describes his playing as a revelation despite his injured hand.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: When you got to Paris, aside from playing in this sort of society, more staid kind of thing, you also were jamming with people like Django Reinhardt.
Can you just tell us a few things about Django and your impressions of him when you first came across him?

Not much. There wasn’t much to know about Django. He was very quiet. He had very little to say. That’s being redundant, isn’t it? [Berger laughs.] But anyway, he was also maybe a little on the shy side, and maybe that was more because being around American musicians and not speaking English, and we not speaking French very well, you know, that probably was part of his feeling. But I couldn’t tell you very much about him, no more than you would read about him, maybe, certainly not as much, because the people that have
known him much better than I did have written rather widely about him, like, for instance, the Charles Delaunay’s book, you know, on Django Reinhardt. But I didn’t know him well.
What about your impressions of his playing? Was this sort of a revelation, that someone in your . . .

Oh, sure. Sure, it was a revelation, as it was to everyone. You know, it was most unusual, and especially with his, oh, what would you call it? His . . . I guess what you would call a handicap was certainly no handicap to him, and that meant the absence of the use of two of his left fingers on his left hand. But for some reason he overcame that and, boy, how he did.
